svg.aria-label: Diagram: the two families of Firewall Insights, with shadowed rules derived from configuration alone and re-evaluated every twenty-four hours while the overly permissive and deny insights are derived from Firewall Rules Logging; the four overly permissive insight subtypes; why the log dependency makes the tool under-report rather than over-report, since a count is accurate only if logging ran for the whole observation period, only TCP and UDP traffic is analysed, and Cloud Monitoring stores no time series at all for a rule that had no hits; the observation period controls and how fast each insight responds to a change; and the machine learning predictions plus the health check ranges that look unused and must not be deleted
svg.title: Firewall Insights: which half comes from configuration, which half comes from logs, and why the log half under-reports
svg.text: Half of these insights read your configuration. The other half read your logs.
The log half is only as complete as your logging was, and it errs toward saying nothing is wrong.
Two families, one insight type
CONFIGURATION-BASED: shadowed rules. No logs needed, no observation period, because it
does not evaluate historical data. Re-evaluated every 24 hours.
LOG-BASED: the four overly permissive insights, plus deny rules with hits.
A shadowed rule shares attributes with another rule of HIGHER OR EQUAL priority, resolved
through #74’s evaluation order — so a policy rule can be shadowed by a VPC rule.
The four ways a rule is called overly permissive
1. Allow rules with NO HITS during the observation period.
2. Allow rules OBSOLETE by adaptive analysis — the usage pattern changed, not stopped.
3. Allow rules with UNUSED ATTRIBUTES — the rule is hit, an IP or port range is not.
4. Allow rules with OVERLY BROAD IP or port ranges, with a narrower range suggested.
Severity: high for all four. Shadowed rules are medium.
The log dependency, and why it fails quietly in the safe-looking direction
The data is accurate ONLY IF logging was enabled for the ENTIRE observation period.
Otherwise the number of rules in each category COULD BE HIGHER THAN INDICATED.
So a short list is ambiguous: either the estate is clean, or the logs were not there.
ONLY TCP AND UDP are analysed. Other traffic is not, so an ICMP-only rule is invisible.
And the metric cannot answer the question at all: Cloud Monitoring does not store data
about rules that had no hits. A missing time series is not evidence of an unused rule.
Use the INSIGHT for what is unused. Use the METRIC only for what is used.
The observation period is a knob, and each insight reacts at its own speed
Default SIX WEEKS. Configurable from SEVEN DAYS to ONE YEAR.
DENY rules with hits: results update IMMEDIATELY when you change the period.
OVERLY PERMISSIVE: up to 48 HOURS, and until then the old period still applies.
SHADOWED: no period at all; the refresh schedule takes effect 24 hours after you save it.
Lengthening the window does not retroactively create logs you were not collecting.
Two insights carry a machine-learning prediction of future hits, trained on firewall rules in
YOUR OWN ORGANIZATION, and each shows the similar rules behind its guess. Adaptive analysis
can flag a rule after the first week of a 12-month window, long before the window closes.
The one named exception: health check and other Google ranges MIGHT NOT BE HIT AND SHOULD
NOT BE REMOVED. The tool will list them; deleting what it lists is not the job.
Reading insights needs Firewall Recommender Viewer; dismissing one needs Admin.
